title: SUSD: Structured Unsupervised Skill Discovery
one_liner: Split the world into independent moving parts, assign each part its own skills, and nudge the agent to explore all of them.
lead: A robot learns skills by trying things and seeing what happens—no reward signal tells it what to do. Most methods favor simple, repetitive skills because they are easy to measure. SUSD watches which objects or entities the robot can move independently, assigns each one its own skill variable, and steers the agent to exercise all of them. The result: the robot discovers rich, diverse skills that engage every controllable thing in its world.

paras: Imagine a robot in a world with three objects: a ball, a box, and a light. Without any reward signal, how does it learn what it can do? One approach: measure how much the robot changes the world by looking at the distance between its current state and all past states. If the distance is high, the skill is interesting. But this favors simple repetitive tricks—spin in a circle, shake the ball—because they are easy and measurable. Deep behaviors that require moving multiple objects together get buried.

Older methods measure how much a skill controls which objects move, by tracking whether an object's position is predictable from the skill alone. But this does not encourage the agent to explore all objects. A robot might nail down skills for the ball and ignore the box entirely. The world's structure—which objects can move independently—goes unused.

callout.html: Unsupervised skill discovery favors simple, static skills and leaves controllable objects unexplored.

steps.text: Break the state (position, velocity, color) into separate pieces for each object.
Let skill 1 control the ball, skill 2 the box, skill 3 the light.
Agent takes actions; record which skill label and which objects moved.
Dynamic model predicts how much each object was affected by each skill.
Nudge the reward so unused object-skill pairs get more tries.

paras: SUSD changes which skill variables the agent is allowed to influence. Instead of one giant skill variable covering the whole world, each skill variable is pinned to one independent factor—ball, box, or light. This constraint forces the agent to discover separate, specialized behaviors.

hidden.h2: Factor engagement—which parts are being explored
hidden.name: skill-factor engagement score
paras: The hidden quantity SUSD measures is how actively each skill is steering each object. For example, if skill 2 is always changing the box's position but never the light, the engagement score for skill 2 and light is low. This is computed by a dynamic model that learns to predict how much an object moves given a skill label.

The dynamic model is trained on real experience: it sees state pairs (before and after an action) along with the skill label, and learns to predict what changed. Over time, it gets good at saying whether this skill actually moved this object. High prediction accuracy means high engagement.

heat.caption: Darker means the dynamic model predicts high state change for that skill-factor pair; bright means inactive.

reads.html: The dynamic model is just a neural network that takes a skill ID and predicts which objects will move.
Factor engagement is estimated via a learned dynamics model that predicts the change in each state factor conditioned on the skill variable.

paras: The mechanism has two parts. First: by assigning each skill to a separate factor (ball, box, light), the agent naturally learns to make each factor move in different ways. Skill 1 only ever moves the ball, so the agent will try pushing, rolling, and flinging it. Skill 2 only moves the box, so it learns box-specific moves. No skill can do everything, so the agent has to exercise all factors.

Second: the dynamic model watches which skill-factor pairs are actually being explored and which are idle. If skill 4 has never actually changed the light, the model's engagement score for (skill 4, light) stays low. The training loop then adds a bonus when the agent tries skill 4 in situations where it might change the light—like when the light is reachable. This steering nudges the agent toward unexplored pairs, ensuring all factors get explored. The result is a factorized skill set where each skill is specialized and the whole set covers all controllable objects.

stages.s: state split into factors: ball, box, light
dynamic model predicts state change per factor

math.words: total reward = distance between states + lambda times the engagement bonus for unexplored skill-factor pairs
symbols: total reward signal given to the agent
state (position, color, etc.) after and before the action
distance or magnitude (how far apart two states are)
how much to value exploration of new skill-factor pairs (tuning dial)
engagement score for factor f, predicted by dynamic model (0 to 1)
bonus for all underexplored factors (higher when factors are unused)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: State distance: ball moved 15 units, box stayed still, light moved 5 units. Magnitude = 15 + 0 + 5 = 20.

If the agent had ignored the box (skill 2 engagement = 0.1), bonus would be (1 - 0.1) + (1 - 0.2) + (1 - 0.8) = 0.9 + 0.8 + 0.2 = 1.9, reward = 20 + 3 * 1.9 = 25.7—higher reward for exploring the idle box skill.

math.note: The bonus term rewards trying skills on factors where the dynamic model says engagement is low, steering the agent toward gaps in exploration.

items.html: If the state split is wrong (say, grouping ball and box together when they move independently), the agent cannot learn which skill controls what. The dynamic model misses the real structure.

If the model is too flexible or trained on short episodes, it may learn spurious correlations (skill 3 tends to change the light because the agent happened to use skill 3 near the light). The engagement scores become misleading, wasting exploration on false leads.
If the exploration bonus weight (lambda) is too high, the agent wastes effort on hard-to-move factors even when they are not useful. Too low, and it reverts to favoring easy factors.

With a correct factorization, a dynamic model that avoids overfitting, and a balanced lambda, the agent explores all factors and learns rich, compositional skills suitable for downstream hierarchical tasks.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple environment with 3–5 independent moving objects (e.g., balls and boxes on a 2D grid, or a simulated arm with movable objects). Assign each object its own skill variable (e.g., skill 1 pushes the ball, skill 2 pushes the box, skill 3 pushes the light). Run SUSD for 100,000 environment steps. Record, for each skill-object pair, how often the skill changed that object's position (e.g., distance moved > 0.5 units after the action). Measure the 'coverage' of each skill: the fraction of objects it can change. Compare against a naive method that uses a single shared skill variable.
demo.metric_eq: coverage = mean over skills of (count of objects that skill can move / total objects)
demo.closing: The demo must show that SUSD achieves high coverage across all objects, while the naive method covers only 1–2 objects per skill.
